title: The Borrowed Regiment
premise: In 1914 Kent, Zephyrine Fairweather, a driver and letter-reader for the formidable suffragist Lady Verity Ashcombe, has built a life on being unremarkable—portable, forgettable, safe. When a young German boy, Emil, is left at the manor door with a note instructing Lady Verity to forget the face of the woman who left him, Zephyrine recognizes the handwriting as that of Greta Lindqvist, a German correspondent whose wartime letters she has been secretly reading and answering. As suspicion of 'enemy aliens' tightens and a local magistrate hunts for the boy, Zephyrine must choose between the invisibility that has protected her and the found family forming around a child she was told to forget. The story ends with Zephyrine testifying at an inquiry, sacrificing her anonymity and her position to secure Emil's guardianship under Lady Verity—choosing, at last, to be seen.
about_author: Marguerite Galloway is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing wartime letters in English county records. She writes historical fiction about the people history filed under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. We meet her packing and unpacking Lady Verity's campaign trunks, measuring her life in portable things, and quietly reading the letters she drives to the post. The emotional beat is the comfort—and loneliness—of being indispensable and invisible at once.

chapters.title: The Letters She Shouldn't Answer
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Among the correspondence she finds letters from Greta Lindqvist in Germany, a pre-war pen friend of Lady Verity's whose replies now require censorship. Zephyrine begins answering in the margins, telling herself it's harmless. Beat: the dangerous intimacy of borrowed words.

chapters.title: A Child at the Door
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, dawn. A boy of about seven stands on the step with a note: 'Forget the face.' The handwriting is Greta's. Emil speaks little, carries a tin soldier, and flinches at the word 'German.' Beat: shock hardening instantly into protectiveness.

chapters.title: The House Learns to Hold Three
chapters.summary: Rotating POV—Zephyrine, the cook Mrs. Pargeter, and Lady Verity. The household improvises a story: Emil is a war orphan from Belgium. Small kindnesses accumulate; Zephyrine teaches him to read from suffrage pamphlets. Beat: found family assembling itself before anyone admits it.

chapters.title: The Magistrate's Visit
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Mr. Halloway, a local magistrate and rival of Lady Verity's, arrives investigating 'enemy persons' after a neighbor's report. Zephyrine lies smoothly for the first time in her careful life and realizes how good she is at it. Beat: fear sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Greta's Confession
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, interleaved with Greta's letters. We learn Greta sent Emil to England to save him from her conscripted husband's family and a country turning on her; the letters reveal she once saved Zephyrine's brother from a Prussian prison, a debt Zephyrine never knew. Beat: the promise becomes personal.

chapters.title: What Mrs. Pargeter Saw
chapters.summary: Mrs. Pargeter's POV. The cook, who has guessed everything, must decide whether to protect the lie when Halloway's clerk comes snooping in the kitchen. She burns a letter, then regrets nothing. Beat: loyalty outweighing caution; the conspiracy of the household deepens.

chapters.title: The Face They Remember
chapters.summary: Lady Verity's POV. Halloway produces a witness—the woman who left Emil, now detained as an enemy alien, who identified the manor. Verity must weigh her cause, her reputation, and the boy. She chooses Emil, and orders Zephyrine to prepare to run. Beat: the mentor's sacrifice reframes the stakes.

chapters.title: The Inquiry
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Climax. At the county inquiry, Zephyrine abandons her invisibility: she confesses to reading the letters, producing Greta's correspondence as proof of Emil's rescue, and names herself as the one who promised to keep him. Halloway's case collapses on her testimony. Beat: the cost and glory of being seen.

chapters.title: Everything Worth Keeping
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, spring 1915. Emil is legally in Lady Verity's care; Zephyrine keeps her post, no longer the woman who could be carried out with the trunks. A final letter arrives from Greta—alive, grateful. Zephyrine reads it aloud at the supper table. Beat: belonging, chosen and declared.
